abstract: |
  We describe a rule-based expert system that classifies Swedish text as written in
  Swedish or translated from English. It consists of 49 hand-written rules over regular
  expressions, word lists and counts, grouped into seven families. Each rule contributes a
  log-likelihood ratio whose parameters were typed by hand from training-split statistics,
  and every verdict comes with span-level evidence. On Europarl v7 with a date-based split
  and topic words masked, the engine reaches accuracy / ROC-AUC of .613 / .666 on single
  sentences, .747 / .833 on 100-token chunks and .920 / .977 on 500-token chunks of the
  held-out validation period (2004–2006), against an AUC of .583, .671 and .792 for a
  sentence-length baseline. Logistic regression and gradient-boosted trees over the same
  expert features add between .006 and .036 AUC. Several literature claims about
  translationese, among them explicitation through connectives, do not hold in this corpus.

# Introduction

Translationese, the set of statistical properties that distinguish translated text from text
originally written in the same language, was named in a study of exactly this language
pair: Swedish novels translated from English [@gellerstam1986]. Computational work has since
shown that translated text can be separated from original text with high accuracy on long
chunks [@baroni2006; @koppel2011; @volansky2015], mostly with function-word, character and
part-of-speech n-gram features in supervised classifiers. For Swedish Europarl, the only
classifier we are aware of is a three-class SVM (original Swedish, from English, from other
languages) over POS and character n-grams on about 2,000-token
chunks, which reached 94.1% in cross-validation and 80% on a held-out set [@joelsson2016].

This report describes a system built under a different constraint: it is fully rule-based.
It uses tokenisation, regular expressions, word lists, counts and hand-written rules with
hand-set parameters, and no trained model, tagger or parser. The rules implement features
from the translation-studies literature (interference, normalisation, unique items,
explicitation) and from contrastive Swedish–English grammar, and each verdict is explained
by the rules that fired and the words they fired on. We evaluate it on the Swedish side of
Europarl with a date-based split, measure how much an ML model on top of the same features
gains, and report which literature claims hold and which do not in this corpus.

The project's literature review (`docs/literature.md`) records how each cited source was
checked. Some were confirmed only through citing sources, among them @gellerstam1986,
@baker1993 and @tirkkonencondit2004; claims attributed to them here follow those secondary
accounts.

# Task and data {#sec-data}

**Corpus and labels.** The data is the Swedish side of Europarl v7 [@koehn2005]. Label 0
marks a speech given in Swedish, label 1 a speech given in English and translated into
Swedish by the European Parliament. Europarl records a speech's source language mainly in
the *other* language versions: a naive reading of the `LANGUAGE` attribute in the Swedish
files finds only 154 original Swedish turns. Labels therefore combine the attribute in
`txt/sv` and `txt/en` (same file, same speaker ID) with inline `(XX)` language markers. A
turn is dropped when these sources disagree, when the Swedish and English
speaker names disagree, or when the text does not look Swedish. Turns in other source
languages and untagged turns are dropped as well. Of 196,477 speaker turns, 5,994 original
and 34,149 translated turns are kept. Tag inconsistency across language files is a known
source of label noise in Europarl [@ustaszewski2019].

**Units.** Three granularities are built: sentences of at least three tokens; and chunks of
consecutive sentences of one class within one session date, emitted as soon as they reach
100 or 500 whitespace tokens (leftovers are dropped). The translated class is several times
larger than the original class, so balanced files downsample it with a fixed seed. All
figures in this report are on balanced files.

**Split and protocol.** The split is by session date, so a session never straddles a cut
(Table&nbsp;\ref{tab-data}). Each split also falls into a different period: trn covers 1997 to mid-2004,
val the following parliamentary term after the 2004 enlargement, test 2007–2011. Speakers
overlap little: of 151 distinct original-language speakers in trn and 89 in val, 10 occur in
both. The protocol is enforced by the tools:

- **trn** is the only split whose texts are read. Rule values are read off trn statistics,
  and examples, keyword-in-context lines and errors are inspected only on trn.
- **val** is used for aggregate metrics only, a few runs per change. The calibration tools
  refuse it, and error listing is disabled.
- **test** is locked for one final run and has **not been run** for this report.

```{=latex}
\input{assets/tab_data.tex}
```

**Topic masking.** Country, nationality, city, party and politician tokens can be replaced by
a placeholder before scoring. Every result is reported masked and unmasked. A deliberately
topic-keyed baseline must fall to chance under masking, which checks that the mask removes
the topical signal. Masked figures are reported throughout; for the engine they differ from
the unmasked ones by at most .001.

# Method {#sec-method}

## Engine

**Text processing.** Input is normalised (quotation marks, dashes, ellipses, whitespace,
soft hyphens, Unicode NFC) with a character offset map back to the original input. A
rule-based sentence splitter ends sentences at `.`, `!`, `?` and `...` before an upper-case
letter or digit, except after known abbreviations and initials; *Herr talman!* `Mr
President!' is its own sentence, and vocative-only sentences are flagged so that
sentence-position and sentence-length rules can skip them. The tokeniser keeps
abbreviations (*t.ex.*, *bl.a.*), numbers with decimal comma or space separators and
hyphenated compounds (*EU-länderna*) as single tokens. Rules read only from a lazily cached
document object (sentences, tokens, lower-cased words, sentence-initial words, punctuation
counts); regular expressions run on the lower-cased normalised text.

**Rule types.** Every rule returns a log-likelihood ratio in nats,
$\mathrm{LLR} = \ln P(\text{text}\mid T) / P(\text{text}\mid O)$, so that positive values
point to *translated*. Five types cover all rules:

- **HitRule**, for rare, high-precision items such as calques: a fixed LLR per match (or one
  per lexicon entry), $\mathrm{LLR} = \sum_{\text{hits}} \ell_h$. Absence is no evidence.
- **RateRule**, the frequency of an item relative to length under a Poisson model, with
  hand-set rates $r_O, r_T$ per 1000 words. For $k$ hits in $n$ words,
  $$\mathrm{LLR} = k \ln\frac{r_T}{r_O} - n\,\frac{r_T - r_O}{1000}.$$
  The second term is evidence from absence and grows with length.
- **ChoiceRule**, which of two competing variants was chosen (binomial), with $p_O, p_T$ the
  share of variant A among A and B in each class:
  $$\mathrm{LLR} = k_A \ln\frac{p_T}{p_O} + k_B \ln\frac{1-p_T}{1-p_O}.$$
  Conditioning on a choice having been made makes it the most robust type to length and
  topic, but it discards information when the rate of variant B also differs between the
  classes.
- **StatRule**, a per-unit statistic (e.g. words per sentence) modelled as Gaussian per
  class; with a pooled SD the LLR is linear in the mean and decomposes into per-sentence
  shares. The statistics family uses a variant whose SD of the text mean is
  $\sqrt{\sigma^2/n + \tau^2}$, where $\tau$ is between-text variation that does not shrink
  with length, so the evidence saturates on long texts.
- **PredicateRule**, arbitrary code returning an LLR, used for the word-order rules (clause
  opening classification over closed word lists for finite verbs, subject pronouns and
  fronted adverbials).

**Combination.** Each rule's LLR is multiplied by a weight $w_r$ (default 1) and clipped to
$\pm c_r$. Rule contributions are summed per family, the family sum is clipped to $\pm C_f$,
and the score is the sum over families:
$$s = \sum_f \operatorname{clip}\Bigl(\sum_{r \in f} \operatorname{clip}(w_r\,\mathrm{LLR}_r,\ \pm c_r),\ \pm C_f\Bigr),
\qquad P(\text{translated}) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-s}}.$$
The prior is 0 (balanced classes) and the decision threshold is $s > 0$. Family caps (2 to
6) bound the damage of correlated rules that read the same tokens.

**Explanations.** Besides the score, the engine reports each rule's contribution (with a
pseudo-entry for the amount a family cap removed, so the contributions sum to the score), a
human-readable evidence sentence per rule, and character spans for every piece of
evidence, mapped back to the original input. Each span carries its signed share of the
rule's contribution; what is not tied to a span (the absence term of rate rules, residuals
of statistics) is reported at document level. Section&nbsp;[-@sec-examples] shows this output.

## Calibration protocol {#sec-calibration}

Rule values are set by hand, as a knowledge engineer would. A rule's pattern and its
rationale are written before any numbers are looked at. A helper tool then prints per-class
statistics on trn (by default the balanced 500-token file, about 0.7M words per class): hits,
rate per 1000 words, share of texts with a hit, variant shares for choices, random
keyword-in-context lines, the share of hits from the five most frequent speakers, and
per-year rates. The KWIC lines are read to check that the pattern matches what was meant,
and the rounded values (at most two significant digits) are typed into the rule with a
comment recording what was seen. There is no automated fitting and no search over
weights, caps or thresholds. Further constraints: every rule cites a literature entry or is
marked as expert judgement; names of countries, parties, persons, cities and institutions
are banned from patterns; every rule is checked for speaker concentration (the share of
hits from the five most frequent speakers); and drifting items get small caps. Values were set on trn, and val was scored a handful of times
to compare rule sets.

## Integration of the families {#sec-integration}

The seven families were calibrated separately and then combined, so evidence that two
families read off the same tokens was initially counted twice. To find such overlaps, every
trn text was scored with all rules and two diagnostics were computed: the within-class
Pearson correlation of every pair of rule contributions (separately in O and T, on 14,170
100-token and 2,734 500-token chunks), and the character overlap of their evidence spans.
Pairs with same-direction $|r| > .3$ or shared spans were resolved by hand, by removing the
overlapping pattern from one rule, disabling one rule, or halving one weight. For example,
a register-family rate of *av* correlated at $r = .96$ (O) and .94 (T) with the
statistics family's *av* rule and was disabled, and sentence-initial *Därför*, *Dessutom*
were removed from the connective rule because the word-order family scores the same tokens
as a topicalised opening. Of 60 defined rules, 49 are enabled. On trn (masked), resolution
moved 100-token AUC from .902 to .907. Family caps bind almost only on 500-token chunks
(particles on 20.0% of original chunks, calques on 11.7% of translated ones), the clipped
amount points to the true class in 90–100% of these cases, and lifting any one cap changes
trn accuracy by 0 and AUC by at most .0002; no cap was changed.

# Features {#sec-features}

Table&nbsp;\ref{tab-features} lists the main rules with their hand-set class parameters; all 49 rules are in
Appendix&nbsp;[-@sec-appendix]. The families are:

- **starter**: modal particles (*ju, nog, väl, visst*) and words per sentence.
- **connectives and punctuation**: native connective adverbs and additive *också* (O),
  Swedish stock equivalents of English discourse markers (*i synnerhet* ‘in particular’, *i
  själva verket* ‘in fact’), sentence-initial *Och/Men*, a comma after a fronted adverbial
  (*Dessutom, vi måste* ‘Moreover, we must’), comma habits around clausal conjunctions,
  dropped complementiser *att* and relative *som*, written-out abbreviations, dash-delimited
  asides, parentheses and exclamation marks.
- **register**: lexical choices between native variants, e.g. *kommer att* vs *ska/skall*
  for the future, *skulle vilja* vs *vill*, *tycka* vs *anse*, *väldigt* vs *mycket*, and
  rates of *bland annat*, *samt*, evaluative *bra*, *självklart* and *den/det/de här*.
- **particles and pronouns**: clause-internal particles (*nämligen, ändå, alltså*, anaphoric
  *då*), stance adverbs, Swedish particle verbs (*slå fast*, *lyfta fram*), generic *man*,
  copular *det är*, possessive and personal pronouns, *ni* vs *man*.
- **calques**: a lexicon of \nCalques{} English calques with per-entry LLRs (*det faktum
  att* ‘the fact that’, *när det rör* ‘as regards’, *de av oss som* ‘those of us who’, *i det
  förflutna* ‘in the past’), two native counterparts, *försöka att* + infinitive, and
  pied-piped relatives (*i vilket* ‘in which’).
- **word order**: a heuristic classifier of main-clause openings (topicalised adverb, object
  or clause with V2 inversion vs subject-first), and English order leaking into Swedish (no
  inversion after a fronted adverbial, V3, main-clause negation order in subordinate
  clauses).
- **statistics**: the share of long words (the LIX criterion) and the share of *av* ‘of, by’
  after nominalisations and elsewhere; these abstain below 50 words.

Sentence examples carry an English gloss.

```{=latex}
\input{assets/examples.tex}
```

The examples show the two main error sources. False positives are originals in an
institutional register that shares the conventions of translated EP prose (Examples 3 and
6), and false negatives are translations in which the translator chose native variants
(Example 4). In both cases, the engine's evidence is correct about the words; the words do
not determine the source language.

# Results {#sec-results}

## Classification

Table&nbsp;\ref{tab-results} and Figure&nbsp;\ref{fig-auc} give accuracy and AUC on trn and val. The engine separates the
classes well on 500-token chunks (val AUC .977) and moderately on single sentences (.666),
where most rules have no hit. It outperforms the mean-sentence-length baseline at every
length. The trn-minus-val AUC gap is .057 for sentences, .074 for 100-token chunks and .013
for 500-token chunks. Since val lies in a later parliamentary term, this gap combines
overfitting of the hand calibration with drift: several markers of original Swedish become
rarer from 1997 to 2004, and short texts depend on single clues more than long ones.

## Family ablation {#sec-ablation}

Table&nbsp;\ref{tab-ablation} removes one family at a time on trn. The ranking by AUC loss at 100 tokens is
connectives and punctuation ($-.030$), register ($-.025$), particles ($-.021$), calques and
the starter rules ($-.011$ each), word order ($-.005$) and statistics ($-.002$). The
statistics family abstains below 50 words and its evidence is largely carried by other
families once all are combined. Word order has a small marginal effect, spread over many
weak per-sentence opening terms; it is kept because it owns the prefield evidence that was
removed from other rules during integration.

## Machine learning on the expert features {#sec-hybrid}

To measure how far the hand-set weights are from learned ones, and how much signal the
expert features carry beyond the engine, we fitted logistic regression (LR), gradient-boosted
trees (GBT) and shallow decision trees on trn (hyper-parameters by five-fold cross-validation
inside trn, folds grouped by session date) and scored each model once on val (Table&nbsp;\ref{tab-hybrid}).
The inputs are expert features only: the engine's per-rule contributions, the raw statistic
each rule computes, and about 110 features from the literature word lists. An LR over the
300 most frequent words serves as a reference without expert input. None of these models
is part of the engine.

```{=latex}
\input{assets/tab_hybrid.tex}
```

Three observations follow. First, **re-weighting the hand-set rules gains little**: an LR
over the 49 rule contributions changes val AUC by +.003, +.007 and $-.005$ at the three
lengths. The learned multiplier on each hand-set contribution is positive for every rule at
every length (no rule changes sign); on 100-token chunks it ranges from \multMinHund{} to
\multMaxHund{}, and \multInHund{} of 49 rules lie between 0.5 and 2. The largest multipliers
(sentence-initial *Men* 2.385, additive *också* 2.067, *den/det/de här* 2.017) mark rules
whose hand-set weights are conservative. The smallest (*tycka* vs *anse* 0.395, *att*-drop
0.446, *ni* vs *man* 0.455) concern rules that share evidence with other rules: *tycker
jag är* fires both *tycka* and *att*-drop, and every generic *man* counts in both *ni* vs
*man* and the generic-*man* rate. Second, **gains come from
additional features**, not from weights: models that add the literature features gain
.035 AUC on sentences, .036 on 100-token chunks and .006 on 500-token chunks over the
engine. Third, **expert features match word frequencies once topic is masked**: the
bag-of-words model is the only one that loses AUC under masking (.707 to .700 on
sentences, .880 to .870 on 100-token chunks). Masked, it is level with the best expert
models on sentences (.700 vs .701) and 100-token chunks (.870 vs .869) and below them on
500-token chunks (.971 vs .983).

# Findings on Swedish translationese in Europarl {#sec-findings}

The calibration statistics give a description of EN→SV translationese in EP proceedings of
1997–2004. Unless stated otherwise, figures are hand-set rule values or calibration statistics on trn
(rates per 1000 words, mostly from 500-token chunks; shares for choices), original vs
translated.

**Unique items are under-represented in translation**, as predicted by the unique-items
hypothesis [@tirkkonencondit2004] and contrastive work on Swedish modal particles
[@aijmer1996]. Modal particle *ju* occurs at 0.96 vs 0.054; the rules for *nämligen* (0.42
vs 0.02), *bland annat* (0.64 vs 0.021) and stance adverbs such as *egentligen* (0.51 vs
0.12) are among the strongest O evidence. Swedish-specific lexical choices behave the same
way: *tycka* takes .58 of *tycka*+*anse* in originals and .2 in translations, *väldigt*
.43 vs .1 of *väldigt*+*mycket* before adjectives, and generic *man* is more frequent in
originals (3.5 vs 2.4).

**Interference from English is visible in function words and fixed phrases.** The future
with *kommer att* (English *will*) takes .24 of *kommer att*+*ska/skall* in originals and .6
in translations; *skulle vilja* (‘would like to’) .097 vs .32 of *skulle vilja*+*vill*; the
non-reflexive possessives *hans/hennes/deras/dess* occur at 0.98 vs 2.8. A comma after a
fronted adverbial follows 1% of such adverbials in originals and 9.1% in translations.
The preposition *av* is more frequent in translations (13.6 vs 19), in line with
@nilsson2004. Translations have longer sentences (mean 18.3 vs 21.5 words), the direction
@volansky2015 report for English. Word order matches the prediction that translators keep
the English theme [@hasselgard2004; @bohnacker2008] only in part: topicalisation leans
original when it is a Swedish-initiated choice (deictic or causal adverbs, object *det*,
*Det vet vi* ‘that know we’), whereas fronted adverbial clauses and structuring conjuncts
(*För det första* ‘firstly’, *Slutligen* ‘finally’) lean translated, since they mirror an
English sentence-initial adverbial. Subject-pronoun-first openings lean translated in
1997–2001, and the difference fades by 2002–2004.

**Claims that do not hold in this corpus:**

- *Explicitation through connectives* [@blumkulka1986; @volansky2015]. The T-leaning
  connectives of the catalogue are *less* frequent in translations (7.02 vs 4.96), and the
  native connective adverbs in the middle field are a strong O feature (4.7 vs 1.9).
- *Normalisation towards formal variants* as reported for EP Swedish by @danielsson2003.
  *skall* and *ska* together occur at 6.4 vs 2.8, so the modal is an O feature; under the EP
  house style of the period, *skall* takes at least 98% of the two in both classes (share of
  *ska* .0022 vs .014).
  *emellertid* (0.55 vs 0.59) and *huruvida* (0.089 vs 0.13) show no usable difference, and
  *således* is more frequent in originals (0.13 vs 0.050). *den/det/de här*, an O keyword
  in that study, is more frequent in translations (0.17 vs 0.90). Formal *samt* leans
  original (0.85 vs 0.25), and so do *naturligtvis/givetvis/självklart* taken together
  (1.2 vs 0.529); only within the choice *naturligtvis* vs *givetvis/förstås* is
  *naturligtvis* the translated variant (.71 vs .85). Danielsson compared EP translations
  with debates of the Swedish Riksdag, not with EP originals, which may explain part of
  the difference.
- *Simplification* [@baker1993; @laviosa1998]. Lexical variety is equal at two significant
  digits: MATTR over 50-word windows .830 vs .828, OVIX 64.3 vs 63.5.
- *Translations avoid sentence-initial conjunctions*, predicted by analogy with English
  [@volansky2015]: sentence-initial *Och* (0.016 vs 0.17) and *Men* (0.45 vs 0.85) are more
  frequent in translations.
- Resumptive *så* after a fronted clause is not an O feature, and *Det är därför* `that is
  why' leans original rather than translated.
- Most textbook calques have no translation lean in EP Swedish: *i termer av*, *på basis
  av*, *i ljuset av*, *baserat på* and *sist men inte minst*. *implementera* occurs almost
  only in originals (0.039 vs 0.0003).

Two properties of the corpus explain much of this. The originals are edited transcripts of
speeches, so spoken-register items (particles, *väldigt*, *bra*, exclamations) mark them;
and the translations are produced under institutional norms of EU Swedish that favour
source-shaped, nominal prose [@bendegard2014]. Features that separate the classes here
may therefore separate speech from institutional writing as much as originals from
translations.

# Limitations {#sec-limitations}

- **One domain.** The rules were built for and tested on edited European Parliament
  proceedings. Some rules partly encode EP or transcription conventions and say so in their
  rationale (written-out abbreviations, dash-delimited asides, exclamation marks). Nothing
  has been tested on fiction, news or other genres, where cross-domain accuracy of
  translationese classifiers is known to drop [@rabinovich2015].
- **Drift.** Several markers of original Swedish decline over 1997–2004, and the rule
  values reflect that period. Val already scores below trn; test (2007–2011) is likely to
  score lower again.
- **Speaker mix.** The originals come from a limited set of Swedish MEPs (151 distinct
  speakers in trn), while the translated class is dominated by European Commission
  speakers. Rule hits were checked for speaker concentration, but the confound cannot be
  removed entirely; Example 6 shows an original that reads like translated Commission
  prose.
- **Short texts.** A single sentence carries little evidence: val AUC is .666 on sentences
  against .977 on 500-token chunks.
- **Labels.** Source-language tags are incomplete and partly inconsistent across language
  versions; the cross-checks drop inconsistent turns but cannot detect relay translation.
- **Test not run.** All held-out figures are from val, which was used, sparingly, to
  compare rule sets. The locked test split (2007–2011, 589 + 589 500-token chunks) has not
  been scored.
